summary.text: Theseus' son by an Amazon — Antiope or Hippolyte in the rival lists — scorned women and was destroyed when Phaedra falsely accused him and Poseidon sent a bull from the sea to wreck his chariot; the queen hanged herself.

chapters.title: The Amazon's son
chapters.text: By the Amazon he had carried off when her sisters marched on Athens — Antiope, Melanippe, or Hippolyte in the rival lists — Theseus begot Hippolytus, a youth who devoted himself to Artemis and would have nothing to do with Aphrodite or the company of women.

chapters.title: Phaedra's false charge
chapters.text: Theseus wedded Phaedra, daughter of Minos, and she bore him two sons — but fell in love with Hippolytus. When he fled her embraces she tore open her chamber, rent her garments, and told Theseus the youth had assaulted her. The king believed the lie and prayed to Poseidon that his son might die.
chapters.citation: Apollod. Epit. 1.18; Ov. Met. 15.500–505; Hyg. Fab. 47

chapters.title: The bull from the sea
chapters.text: As Hippolytus drove his chariot beside the shore, Poseidon sent up a bull from the surf; the horses bolted, the car was shattered, and the youth, tangled in the reins, was dragged to death. Phaedra hanged herself — when the truth came out, in Apollodorus; in Hyginus, as soon as her letter had accused him. Apollodorus counts Hippolytus among the dead whom Asclepius raised — the art for which Zeus struck the healer down — and Ovid has Diana hide the restored youth as Virbius in her sacred grove.
chapters.citation: Apollod. Epit. 1.19; Apollod. 3.10.3–4; Ov. Met. 15.506–546; Hyg. Fab. 47
